The quantity consumers are willing and able to buy at each price per period, ceteris paribus. Desire must be backed by ability to pay.
Ceteris paribus, a higher price leads to a lower quantity demanded, and vice versa: an inverse relationship.
Price of a good falls. Movement or shift? What is it called?
Movement down along the demand curve: an expansion (increase in quantity demanded).
Name five non-price determinants of demand.
Price of substitutes/complements, income, tastes & preferences, expected future price, government policy (also population, credit).
Price of coffee rises. What happens to demand for tea (a substitute)?
Demand for tea increases: D shifts right, because tea is now relatively cheaper.
Price of petrol falls. Effect on demand for cars?
Cars and petrol are complements, so demand for cars increases (shifts right).
What is an inferior good? Example?
Demand falls as income rises, e.g. bus tickets, second-hand clothes. YED < 0.
A status good whose quantity demanded may rise as price rises because high price signals prestige (diamonds, luxury watches).
What is a Giffen good and why does demand slope up?
A staple inferior good taking a large share of poor households' income. A price rise makes them too poor to buy better foods, so they buy more of the staple.
The quantity producers are willing and able to sell at each price per period, ceteris paribus.
Wages rise. What happens to supply?
Costs rise → supply decreases → S shifts left (up).
How does a specific tax differ from an ad valorem tax on the diagram?
Specific: fixed amount per unit → parallel upward shift. Ad valorem: % of price → pivots, gap widens at higher prices.
What does a subsidy do to supply?
Lowers costs per unit → S shifts right/down by the subsidy amount.
Beef and leather: what relationship? Effect of higher beef demand on leather?
Joint supply. More beef produced → supply of leather shifts right → leather price falls.
Oranges rise in price. Effect on lemon supply (competitive supply)?
Farmers shift land to oranges → supply of lemons decreases (shifts left).
The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, with no tendency to change.
Price is above equilibrium. What exists and what happens?
Excess supply (surplus); sellers cut price until Qd = Qs.
Demand and supply both increase. What is certain?
Quantity rises for certain. Price depends on which shift is bigger.
Demand rises and supply falls. What is certain?
Price rises for certain. Quantity depends on the relative size of the shifts.
PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP. 0.2 = inelastic: a 1% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 0.2%.
Demand is inelastic. Should a firm raise or lower price to raise revenue?
Raise it: quantity falls proportionally less than price rises, so TR rises.
Where on a straight-line demand curve is PED = 1?
At the midpoint, where TR is maximised. Above it demand is elastic; below it inelastic.
Substitutes (most important), proportion of income, necessity vs luxury, habit/addiction, time period (and breadth of definition).
Why do governments tax goods with inelastic demand?
Quantity falls little, so tax revenue is high (price rises proportionally more than quantity falls).
Define PES and give its formula.
Responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price, ceteris paribus. PES = %ΔQs ÷ %ΔP.
Spare capacity, stocks/storability, mobility of factors, time period, nature of the good (primary vs manufactured).
Why is agricultural supply price inelastic?
Growing seasons mean output cannot be raised quickly, and perishability limits stocks.
A straight supply curve through the origin has PES = ?
Inferior good: demand falls as income rises.
How can a firm use YED?
Plan output over the business cycle, diversify the product range (luxury to no-frills), adjust marketing in booms vs recessions.
%ΔQd of good A ÷ %ΔP of good B.
Main determinant of the size of XED?
How closely the goods are related (closeness as substitutes or complements).
Two general limitations of any elasticity estimate.
Based on past data that may be unreliable or out of date; ceteris paribus rarely holds in reality.
Define consumer surplus and where it sits on the diagram.
Maximum price willing to pay minus price paid. Area below D and above the price.
Define producer surplus and where it sits.
Price received minus minimum price acceptable (marginal cost). Area above S and below the price.
Willing to pay $1.00 and $0.90 for two drinks priced $0.75. Total CS?
Costs rise and price rises. When is the loss of CS largest in absolute terms?
When demand is price inelastic: price rises most, so buyers pay much more per unit.
Name the three functions of the price mechanism.
Explain the rationing function with a diagram reference.
Supply falls → price rises → movement up D → the good goes to those willing and able to pay most.
What is the transmission of preferences?
The automatic way prices let consumers' wants be known to producers (part of the signalling function).
Higher prices make production more profitable, so firms expand output and hire resources: a movement up the supply curve.
Demand for a factor that comes from demand for the product it makes, e.g. supermarket workers.
Mark split of a 12-mark part (b), and the penalty for one-sided answers?
AO1+AO2 8, AO3 4. One-sided: capped at Level 2 for AO1/AO2 and 0 for AO3.
What makes a conclusion earn AO3 marks?
A judgement that answers the exact question, supported by reasons and conditions ("on balance… because… unless…").
Buffer stock: what does the agency do in a good harvest?
Buys the surplus at the target price and stores it, preventing price falling below the target.
